conflicts/spanish-civil-war/name: The Spanish Civil War: “crusade” and anticlerical terror
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/religionRole: The war was fought over class, land, regional autonomy, the army’s place and the survival of a democratic republic, not over doctrine. But religion was one of its deepest fault lines. The Church was identified with the old order, and in the Republican zone revolutionary militias killed nearly 7,000 clergy and religious and burned thousands of churches in the summer of 1936. The insurgent Nationalists, in turn, adopted the language of ‘crusade’ with the blessing of most bishops, and Catholicism became the core of Franco’s ideology. Historians such as Paul Preston stress that the ‘crusade’ label legitimised a military rebellion and its own mass repression; others, such as Julius Ruiz and Mary Vincent, emphasise how far anticlerical violence was a deliberate revolutionary project. Religion was thus a major driver of mobilisation and violence on both sides, though rarely the original cause of the war.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/sides/0/name: Republicans (Popular Front government, socialists, anarchists, communists, Basque and Catalan nationalists)
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/sides/0/fait: Largely secular or anticlerical; Basque nationalists were devoutly Catholic
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/summary: The military rising of July 1936 against Spain’s Second Republic triggered a revolution and a three-year civil war. In the Republican zone nearly 7,000 priests, monks and nuns were murdered and churches burned; in the Nationalist zone, a far larger repression of perceived leftists was carried out under a cause that bishops proclaimed a ‘crusade’. Franco’s victory in 1939 created a National-Catholic dictatorship that lasted until 1975.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/story:
The Second Republic, proclaimed in April 1931, set out to break the power of the Church in a country where the Catholic religion had been the religion of the state. The 1931 Constitution separated Church and state, legalised divorce, ended state funding of clergy and, in Article 26, dissolved the Jesuits and barred religious orders from teaching; Manuel Azaña declared that ‘Spain has ceased to be Catholic’. In May 1931 crowds burned convents in Madrid, Málaga and other cities while authorities hesitated. Catholics organised politically in the CEDA, which won the 1933 elections, and the October 1934 revolution in Asturias saw some thirty-four priests and religious killed before the army, under Franco’s direction, crushed it brutally. The Popular Front’s narrow victory in February 1936 was followed by months of strikes, political murders and church burnings.

On 17–18 July 1936 army garrisons in Morocco and across Spain rose against the government. The coup failed in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and the Basque Country, splitting the country. Where it failed, the state’s authority collapsed into the hands of workers’ militias, and a revolutionary terror fell on landowners, right-wing politicians and above all the clergy. Between July and December 1936 thousands of priests, monks and nuns were shot — in Barbastro, Lleida, Toledo, Madrid and across Catalonia and Valencia — including the Bishop of Barbastro, Florentino Asensio, and 51 Claretian seminarians. Churches were burned, tombs desecrated and images destroyed; militiamen staged the ‘execution’ of the Sacred Heart monument at the Cerro de los Ángeles. The Republican government condemned much of this violence but could not control it until 1937.

In the Nationalist zone the repression was planned from the outset by the generals as a ‘cleansing’ of the left. Leftist politicians, union members, teachers, Freemasons and intellectuals, including the poet Federico García Lorca, were shot in their tens of thousands; at Badajoz in August 1936 the Army of Africa killed hundreds, perhaps thousands, after taking the city. Most bishops blessed the rising: Bishop Enrique Plá y Deniel’s pastoral letter ‘The Two Cities’ (September 1936) called it a ‘crusade’, and Cardinal Isidro Gomá of Toledo drafted the Collective Letter of the Spanish Bishops of 1 July 1937, which justified the war to the Catholic world. Yet the Nationalists also shot at least fourteen Basque priests in 1936 for supporting the Catholic Basque government, and the bombing of Guernica by the German Condor Legion on 26 April 1937 divided Catholic opinion abroad.

The war became an international struggle. Germany and Italy sent troops, aircraft and arms to Franco; the Soviet Union armed the Republic, and International Brigades of volunteers fought for it, while Britain and France pursued non-intervention. The Nationalists relieved the besieged Alcázar of Toledo in September 1936 but failed to take Madrid that winter; during the Madrid siege thousands of right-wing prisoners were massacred at Paracuellos de Jarama in November–December 1936. The Nationalists conquered the Basque Country and the north in 1937, cut the Republic in two in 1938, won the long battle of the Ebro (July–November 1938), took Barcelona in January 1939 and Madrid on 28 March; Franco declared the war over on 1 April 1939.

Victory brought a ‘peace’ of reprisals: perhaps 20,000 Republicans were executed after the war, hundreds of thousands passed through prisons and camps, and around half a million went into exile. The new regime restored the Church’s privileges, its control of education and its moral authority, a system later called National Catholicism. The Concordat of 1953 sealed the alliance. Pope Pius XI had in September 1936 blessed the defenders of religion while also asking them to love their enemies; Pius XII congratulated Franco on his victory in 1939.

From the 1960s, under the influence of the Second Vatican Council, many Spanish Catholics distanced themselves from the regime. In 1971 a Joint Assembly of bishops and priests debated a motion asking pardon for the Church’s failure to be a ministry of reconciliation in the war; it won a majority but not the two-thirds needed. Since 1987 the Catholic Church has beatified more than 2,000 victims of the 1936 persecution, including 498 in 2007 and 522 at Tarragona in 2013, while the Historical Memory Law of 2007 and the Democratic Memory Law of 2022 address the victims of Francoist repression, including the exhumation of Franco from the Valley of the Fallen in 2019.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/nameOfGod: The Nationalist cause was proclaimed a ‘Crusade’ (Cruzada) for God and Spain. Bishop Plá y Deniel’s ‘The Two Cities’ (1936) drew on Augustine to set the city of God against the city of the godless; the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937 called the war an ‘armed plebiscite’ in defence of Christian civilisation. Requetés of the Carlist militia went into battle with the Sacred Heart badge and the cry ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey!’, chaplains accompanied Nationalist units, and Franco presented himself as ‘Caudillo by the grace of God’. On the Republican side, revolutionary anticlericalism attacked the Church as the ideological prop of oppression and sought to eradicate public religion altogether.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/religiousCau: The Church was closely identified with the monarchy, landowners and the right, and anticlericalism had deep roots among Spanish workers and peasants since the nineteenth century.
The Republic’s constitution and laws of 1931–33 dissolved the Jesuits, barred religious orders from teaching and secularised marriage and cemeteries, which Catholics saw as persecution.
Waves of church burnings in 1931, 1934 and 1936 convinced many Catholics that the Republic threatened religion itself.
Catholic political mobilisation through the CEDA and Catholic Action made religion a central axis of electoral conflict.
The bishops’ framing of the rising as a ‘crusade’ gave the Nationalist cause religious legitimacy at home and abroad.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/otherCauses/: Agrarian conflict between large landowners and landless labourers, especially in Andalusia and Extremadura.
Militant labour movements — anarchist, socialist and communist — and fears of revolution after Asturias in 1934.
Army officers’ hostility to military reforms and to Catalan and Basque autonomy.
The European polarisation between fascism and communism, and the intervention of Germany, Italy and the Soviet Union.
Political violence and the breakdown of public order in the spring of 1936.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/triggers/0: The victory of the Popular Front in the elections of February 1936.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/triggers/1: The murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Republican police on 13 July 1936.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/triggers/2: The military coup of 17–18 July 1936 and its partial failure.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/0/t: Proclamation of the Second Republic (April); convent burnings (May); anticlerical Constitution (December).
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/1/t: The Society of Jesus is dissolved in Spain.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/2/t: Revolution in Asturias; some thirty-four priests and religious killed; the army crushes the rising.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/3/t: Popular Front victory (February); military coup (17–18 July); anticlerical killings across the Republican zone; massacre at Badajoz (August).
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/4/t: Plá y Deniel’s ‘The Two Cities’ calls the war a crusade (September); Alcázar of Toledo relieved; Paracuellos massacres (November–December).
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/5/t: Bombing of Guernica (26 April); Collective Letter of the Spanish bishops (1 July); fall of Bilbao and the north.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/6/t: Battle of the Ebro (July–November), the war’s largest battle.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/7/t: Fall of Barcelona (January) and Madrid (28 March); Franco declares victory on 1 April; Pius XII congratulates him.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/8/t: Concordat between Franco’s Spain and the Holy See.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/9/t: Joint Assembly of bishops and priests debates asking pardon for the Church’s role in the war.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/timeline/10/: Beatification of 498 martyrs of 1934–37 and passage of the Historical Memory Law.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/0/: Nationalist commander and head of state
Led the Army of Africa, became Generalísimo in 1936 and directed the war and its repression.
Ruled Spain as dictator until his death in 1975; buried at the Valley of the Fallen until exhumed in 2019.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/1/: Cardinal Archbishop of Toledo and Primate of Spain
Acted as the Nationalists’ informal representative to the Vatican and drafted the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937.
Later clashed with the regime over Nazi influence; died in 1940.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/2/: Bishop of Salamanca, later Archbishop of Toledo
His pastoral letter ‘The Two Cities’ (1936) gave the rising its theology of crusade; he lent Franco his palace as headquarters.
Primate of Spain 1941–68, a pillar of National Catholicism.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/3/: Rescued from the anarchists in 1936 by the Catalan government, he refused to sign the 1937 Collective Letter and worked for mediation.
Franco barred his return to Spain; he died in exile in Switzerland in 1943.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/4/: Expelled by the Nationalists, he protested to the Pope against their execution of Basque priests and did not sign the Collective Letter.
Returned to Spain in 1947 but never to his diocese.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/5/: Arrested by anarchist militias, tortured and shot in August 1936.
Beatified in 1997 as one of the martyrs of the persecution.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/6/: Prime minister and President of the Republic
Architect of the 1931 religious laws; as president during the war he deplored the terror and in 1938 appealed for ‘peace, pity and pardon’.
Died in exile in France in 1940.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/keyPeople/7/: Witnessed the Nationalist repression on Majorca and denounced it in Les Grands Cimetières sous la lune (1938).
Broke with the Catholic right; his book became a landmark of Catholic dissent.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/casualties/n: Total deaths from combat, repression and war-related causes are usually estimated at 350,000–500,000. Antonio Montero Moreno’s count of the anticlerical violence (1961) — 13 bishops, 4,184 diocesan priests and seminarians, 2,365 male religious and 283 nuns, some 6,832 in all — is widely accepted. Paul Preston and others estimate around 50,000 killed in the Republican zone’s repression and about 130,000 in Nationalist repression during the war, plus perhaps 20,000 executions after 1939; these repression figures remain debated as local research continues.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/effects/0: Franco’s dictatorship ruled Spain until 1975, with political parties banned and regional languages suppressed.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/effects/1: Around half a million Spaniards went into exile in 1939, many to France and Mexico.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/effects/2: The war served as a proving ground for German and Italian air power and tactics before the Second World War.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/effects/3: The memory of the war — exhumations, monuments and the Valley of the Fallen — remains politically divisive in Spain.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/effectsOnChu: The Church regained privileges, control of education and moral censorship under National Catholicism, sealed in the 1953 Concordat.
The killing of nearly 7,000 clergy and religious left a lasting memory of martyrdom, expressed in more than 2,000 beatifications since 1987.
The Church’s identification with the victors alienated many Spaniards and contributed to rapid secularisation after 1975.

From the 1960s Catholic workers’ movements, Basque and Catalan clergy and bishops such as Cardinal Vicente Enrique y Tarancón distanced the Church from the regime and supported the transition to democracy.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/legacy: The Spanish Civil War is a classic case of mutual sacralisation: one side making war on religion and the other making war in its name. Catholic opinion abroad split — Bernanos, Maritain and Mounier against the ‘crusade’, many others for it — and the Church in Spain has since struggled to honour its martyrs without appearing to forget the victims of the side it blessed.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/dissenters/0: The Archbishop of Tarragona refused to sign the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937 and pressed the Vatican to promote a negotiated peace and protect civilians on both sides.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/dissenters/1: The Bishop of Vitoria protested to Rome against the Nationalists’ execution of Basque priests and refused to endorse the crusade.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/dissenters/2: The French Catholic novelist, initially sympathetic to the rising, exposed the Nationalist killings on Majorca and the clergy who condoned them.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/dissenters/3: The Catholic philosopher rejected the description of the war as a holy war, arguing in 1937 that it was a sacrilege to call it a holy war and to kill in the name of God.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/dissenters/4: Many Basque priests supported the Republic’s Catholic Basque government against Franco, and some, such as those shot in 1936, paid with their lives.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/theatres/0/n: Barbastro (killing of bishop and Claretian seminarians)
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/theatres/7/n: Salamanca (Nationalist headquarters in the bishop’s palace)
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/campaigns/0/: The Army of Africa’s march on Madrid
Moroccan Regulares and the Spanish Legion under Franco, Juan Yagüe and José Varela

Airlifted across the Strait from July 1936, the colonial army advanced from Seville through Extremadura, massacring prisoners at Badajoz, diverted to relieve the Alcázar of Toledo in September and reached the outskirts of Madrid in November, where its assault was halted.
conflicts/spanish-civil-war/campaigns/1/: The Nationalist campaign in the north
Nationalist armies under Emilio Mola and later Fidel Dávila, with the German Condor Legion and Italian troops

From March 1937 the Nationalists attacked the Catholic Basque Country — bombing Durango and Guernica — took Bilbao in June, Santander in August and Asturias by October, ending the Republic’s northern front.
